category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A major virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus is Protein A. What is the precise pathological mechanism by which this protein facilitates evasion of host defenses?
options: It degrades DNA in necrotic tissue, allowing the organism to spread rapidly through subcutaneous tissue.
It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the binding of the Fc receptor on phagocytes.
It activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then catalyzes the formation of a protective fibrin clot.
It cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, leading to separation of the epidermis at the granular layer.
It acts as a superantigen, causing a massive release of IL-1, IL-2, and TNF from T cells.
correctOption: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the binding of the Fc receptor on phagocytes.
optionExplanations: This describes the function of DNase (streptodornase), which is typically associated with S. pyogenes.
By binding the Fc region of IgG, Protein A orients the antibody 'upside down,' preventing phagocytes from recognizing the Fc tail and initiating opsonization.
This describes the function of coagulase, an enzyme, not Protein A.
This describes the mechanism of exfoliatin, which causes scalded skin syndrome.
This describes the mechanism of superantigens like TSST-1 and enterotoxin.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): (1) Protein A is the major protein in the cell wall. It is an important virulence factor because it binds to the Fc portion of immunoglobulin (Ig) G. The Fc part is occupied and is not free to bind to the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages, so phagocytosis of S. aureus by those cells does not occur.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Mechanism of Immune Evasion by Protein A
statement: A major virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus is Protein A. What is the precise pathological mechanism by which this protein facilitates the evasion of host immune defenses?
options: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing opsonization and phagocytosis.
It forms pores in the cell membrane of neutrophils, leading to cell death.
It cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, causing epidermal separation.
It acts as a superantigen, causing massive release of IL-1 and IL-2.
It activates prothrombin to thrombin, leading to fibrin clot formation.
correctOption: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing opsonization and phagocytosis.
optionExplanations: Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG antibodies. This prevents the antibody from acting as an opsonin because the Fc region is unavailable to bind to Fc receptors on phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages).
This describes the action of P-V leukocidin or alpha toxin, which are pore-forming toxins, not Protein A.
This describes the mechanism of exfoliatin, which causes scalded skin syndrome, not Protein A.
This describes the mechanism of TSST-1 and enterotoxins, which act as superantigens, not Protein A.
This describes the enzymatic function of coagulase, which walls off the bacteria from neutrophils, not Protein A.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): Protein A is the major protein in the cell wall. It is an important virulence factor because it binds to the Fc portion of immunoglobulin (Ig) G. The Fc part is occupied and is not free to bind to the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages, so phagocytosis of S. aureus by those cells does not occur.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Which enzyme produced by Staphylococcus aureus catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot, effectively walling off the site of infection?
options: Hyaluronidase
Coagulase
Lipase
Staphylokinase
Catalase
correctOption: Coagulase
optionExplanations: Hyaluronidase is a 'spreading factor' that breaks down the hyaluronic acid in connective tissue to facilitate bacterial movement.
Coagulase is the definitive marker for S. aureus. It activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin, creating the characteristic walled-off abscess.
Lipase is an enzyme that degrades fats and oils, allowing the bacteria to colonize the sebaceous glands of the skin; it is not involved in clot formation.
Staphylokinase is a fibrinolysin that dissolves clots; it has the opposite effect of the enzyme asked for in the question.
Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; it protects the bacteria from oxidative stress but does not affect the clotting cascade.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 105 (Book Page)-119: S. aureus is distinguished from the others primarily by coagulase production (Figure 15–6). Coagulase is an enzyme that causes plasma to clot by activating prothrombin to form thrombin. Thrombin then catalyzes the activation of fibrinogen to form the fibrin clot.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Initial microbiological differentiation between major Gram-positive cocci.
statement: Which of the following biochemical and microscopic findings most reliably differentiates the genus Staphylococcus from the genus Streptococcus?
options: Presence of a polysaccharide capsule and gram-positive staining.
Ability to form spores and growth in chains.
Production of catalase and arrangement in irregular clusters.
Production of coagulase and the presence of flagella.
Fermentation of mannitol and production of hyaluronidase.
correctOption: Production of catalase and arrangement in irregular clusters.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Both genera are Gram-positive cocci and many species in both can have capsules; this does not serve as a primary genus-level differentiator.
Incorrect. Neither Staphylococcus nor Streptococcus are spore-forming bacteria; only Streptococcus grows in chains.
Correct. Staphylococci are biochemically characterized as catalase-positive (degrading H2O2) and morphologically as grapelike clusters, while streptococci are catalase-negative and form chains.
Incorrect. While coagulase differentiates S. aureus from other staphylococci, it does not define the whole genus; furthermore, both genera are nonmotile and lack flagella.
Incorrect. Mannitol fermentation is primarily a feature of S. aureus, not all staphylococci, and hyaluronidase is produced by several species in both genera.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 104 (Book Page): Both staphylococci and streptococci are gram-positive cocci, but they are differentiated by two main criteria: (1) Microscopically, staphylococci appear in grapelike clus- ters, whereas streptococci are in chains. (2) Biochemically, staphylococci produce catalase (i.e., they degrade hydrogen peroxide), whereas streptococci do not.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Which cell wall component of Streptococcus pyogenes is the primary antiphagocytic factor that functions by inactivating C3b?
options: Lipoteichoic acid
Streptolysin O
Hyaluronic acid capsule
C carbohydrate
M protein
correctOption: M protein
optionExplanations: Lipoteichoic acid mediates the adherence of the streptococci to pharyngeal mucosal cells but does not inactivate the complement system.
Streptolysin O is a pore-forming toxin that kills leukocytes and causes beta-hemolysis, but it does not function primarily as an antiphagocytic cell wall protein.
While the hyaluronic acid capsule does play a role in retarding phagocytosis, the M protein is documented as the most important antiphagocytic factor with a specific C3b-inactivation mechanism.
C carbohydrate is the antigen used for Lancefield grouping (identifying the organism as Group A), but it is not the primary antiphagocytic factor.
M protein is the defining virulence factor for S. pyogenes; it blocks phagocytosis by preventing opsonization via the inactivation of C3b.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 113 (Book Page): M protein is the most important virulence factor of S. pyogenes. It protrudes from the outer surface of the cell and blocks phagocytosis (i.e., it is antiphagocytic). It inactivates C3b, a component of complement that opsonizes the bacteria prior to phagocytosis (see Chapter 63).

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Pathogenesis of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).
statement: A 4-day-old infant is brought to the neonatal intensive care unit with a temperature of 101.5°F, irritability, and widespread areas of erythematous, 'rolled up' desquamated skin that appears burned. There are no actual blisters (bullae) in the primary area of sloughing. The attending physician notes that the damage occurs at the granular cell layer of the epidermis. What is the enzymatic activity of the toxin causing this condition?
options: A lecithinase that degrades cell membranes and lyses erythrocytes.
A protease that specifically cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes.
Pore formation in the leukocyte cell membrane leading to cytoplasmic leakage.
An adenylate cyclase that increases intracellular cAMP to cause fluid efflux.
A glycosidase that stops protein synthesis by removing adenine from 28S rRNA.
correctOption: A protease that specifically cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes the alpha toxin (lecithinase) of Clostridium perfringens, which causes gas gangrene.
Correct. The toxin is exfoliatin (produced by S. aureus), which acts as a protease to cleave desmoglein in desmosomes, causing separation at the granular layer.
Incorrect. This describes the action of alpha-toxin or P-V leukocidin, which cause tissue necrosis and leukocyte death, not diffuse epidermal sloughing.
Incorrect. This is the mechanism of Cholera toxin or B. anthracis edema factor, which cause edema or diarrhea but not skin desquamation.
Incorrect. This describes the mechanism of Shiga toxin, produced by Shigella or EHEC, not Staphylococcus.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): Exfoliatin causes “scalded skin” syndrome in young children. It is “epidermolytic” and acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, leading to the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is characterized by the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer. What is the molecular target of the exfoliatin toxin responsible for this clinical finding?
options: The 28S ribosomal RNA of host cells
Alpha-helical segments of myosin
Elongation factor-2 involved in protein synthesis
The Fc receptor on macrophage membranes
Desmoglein in desmosomes
correctOption: Desmoglein in desmosomes
optionExplanations: Option D is incorrect because the 28S rRNA is the target of Shiga toxin produced by Shigella and certain E. coli strains.
Option A is incorrect because myosin is the target of cross-reacting antibodies in Rheumatic Fever (post-streptococcal), not SSSS.
Option E is incorrect because elongation factor-2 is the target of Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas Exotoxin A.
Option C is incorrect because while Protein A interacts with the Fc portion of IgG, it does not target the Fc receptor on macrophages itself.
Option B is correct. Exfoliatin is a protease that specifically targets and cleaves desmoglein, a protein that maintains the integrity of desmosomes in the skin.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): Exfoliatin causes “scalded skin” syndrome in young children. It is “epidermolytic” and acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, leading to the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Superantigen Pathogenesis in Toxic Shock Syndrome
statement: A 19-year-old female is brought to the emergency department with a sudden onset of high fever (104.2°F), vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Physical examination reveals a diffuse, macular, sunburn-like rash on her trunk and extremities, and a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. Laboratory findings indicate elevated liver enzymes and a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL. She is currently menstruating and using high-absorbency tampons. What is the primary pathological mechanism of the toxin likely responsible for this condition?
options: Pore formation in the cell membrane leading to loss of low-molecular-weight substances
Proteolytic cleavage of desmoglein in the granular layer of the epidermis
Stimulation of the enteric nervous system via serotonin release from mast cells
ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2 to inhibit protein synthesis
Binding to MHC class II and T-cell receptors to trigger massive cytokine release
correctOption: Binding to MHC class II and T-cell receptors to trigger massive cytokine release
optionExplanations: This describes the mechanism of Alpha toxin or P-V leukocidin, which cause localized necrosis or leukocidial effects, not systemic toxic shock.
This describes the mechanism of exfoliatin, which causes scalded skin syndrome, but does not cause the multi-organ failure and hypotension seen here.
This is the mechanism by which S. aureus enterotoxin induces vomiting in food poisoning, but it does not account for the hypotension and multi-organ involvement of TSS.
ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 is the mechanism of Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa toxins, not S. aureus toxins.

Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin (TSST-1) acts as a superantigen by binding non-specifically to the exterior of MHC class II molecules on APCs and the V-beta chain of T-cell receptors. This bypasses normal antigen processing and triggers a 'cytokine storm' of IL-1, IL-2, and TNF, causing shock and organ damage.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): TSST is a superantigen and causes toxic shock by stimulating the release of large amounts of IL-1, IL-2, and TNF.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Which biochemical characteristic is used as the primary definitive criterion to differentiate the genus Staphylococcus from the genus Streptococcus?
options: The arrangement of cocci in chains
The presence of a polysaccharide capsule
The pattern of hemolysis on blood agar
The ability to produce the enzyme catalase
The sensitivity to the antibiotic bacitracin
correctOption: The ability to produce the enzyme catalase
optionExplanations: While microscopic arrangement (clusters vs. chains) is a criterion, the question asks for a biochemical characteristic. Arrangement is a morphological feature, not biochemical.
Polysaccharide capsules are found in both genera (e.g., S. aureus and S. pneumoniae) and cannot be used to distinguish the two entire genera.
Both genera contain species that exhibit alpha, beta, or gamma hemolysis; therefore, hemolysis is a species-specific or group-specific marker, not a genus-level differentiator.
Staphylococci produce catalase, an enzyme that degrades hydrogen peroxide, while all streptococci are catalase-negative. This is the gold-standard biochemical test for genus-level differentiation.
Bacitracin sensitivity is used to identify Group A Streptococci (S. pyogenes) but is not used to differentiate between the broader genera of Staphylococcus and Streptococcus.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 104 (Book Page): All staphylococci produce catalase, whereas no streptococci do (catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O).

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent cause of food poisoning characterized by a short incubation period. What is the precise mechanism by which the enterotoxin induces the hallmark symptom of prominent vomiting?
options: Inhibition of protein synthesis by removing adenine from 28S ribosomal RNA.
Proteolytic cleavage of elongation factor-2 in the mucosal cells.
ADP-ribosylation of G proteins leading to increased cyclic AMP in enterocytes.
Direct invasion of the intestinal mucosa causing ulcerative lesions and hemorrhage.
Stimulation of the enteric nervous system via serotonin release to activate the vomiting center.
correctOption: Stimulation of the enteric nervous system via serotonin release to activate the vomiting center.
optionExplanations: Inhibition of protein synthesis by rRNA modification is the mechanism of Shiga toxin.
Cleavage of EF-2 is the mechanism of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
Increased cyclic AMP is the mechanism for E. coli heat-labile toxin and cholera toxin, not staphylococcal enterotoxin.
Staphylococcal food poisoning is toxigenic, not invasive; the mucosa remains intact and no hemorrhage occurs.
The enterotoxin acts as a superantigen to trigger serotonin release, which signals the CNS vomiting center via the vagus nerve.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): The prominent vomiting is caused by serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) released from mast cells, which stimulates the enteric nervous system via the vagus nerve to activate the vomiting center in the brain.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A neonate presents with fever and widespread areas of erythematous, 'rolled up' desquamated skin. The clinical diagnosis is Scalded Skin Syndrome. Pathologically, what specific action of the causative toxin leads to this presentation?
options: It functions as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the granular cell layer.
It inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2.
It acts as a superantigen inducing the release of Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF).
It degrades DNA in necrotic tissue to facilitate bacterial spread.
It forms transmembrane holes, causing loss of low-molecular-weight substances.
correctOption: It functions as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the granular cell layer.
optionExplanations: The exfoliatin toxin produced by S. aureus is an epidermolytic protease. It specifically targets and cleaves desmoglein, a protein that holds desmosomes together, leading to skin separation.
This is the mechanism of Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A, not any toxin produced by staphylococci.
TNF release is associated with TSST-1 and septic shock, not the localized epidermal sloughing of SSS.
This describes the function of DNase (streptodornase) produced by S. pyogenes.
This describes the cytotoxic mechanism of alpha toxin, not exfoliatin.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): Exfoliatin causes “scalded skin” syndrome in young children. It is “epidermolytic” and acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, leading to the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with periorbital edema, hypertension, and 'smoky' urine. Two weeks earlier, he had a skin infection characterized by honey-colored crusts on his legs. Blood analysis shows an elevated anti-DNase B titer. What is the underlying immunologic mechanism for the patient's current renal condition?
options: Direct invasion of the renal parenchyma by the bacteria
Toxin-mediated cleavage of desmosomes in the granular cell layer
Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane
Cross-reactivity between bacterial M proteins and renal tissue
Superantigen-induced release of IL-2 and TNF from macrophages
correctOption: Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane
optionExplanations: Acute Glomerulonephritis is a nonsuppurative disease; the bacteria do not directly infect the kidney.
This describes the pathology of Scalded Skin Syndrome caused by S. aureus exfoliatin.
Post-streptococcal AGN is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction involving the deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli.
Cross-reactivity with M proteins is the mechanism for Acute Rheumatic Fever, which affects the heart and joints, not the kidney.
This describes the mechanism of Toxic Shock Syndrome, not the immune-mediated sequel of nephritogenic S. pyogenes strains.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 116 (Book Page): The disease [Acute Glomerulonephritis] is initiated by antigen–antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane. Complement is activated and C5a attracts neutrophils that secrete enzymes that damage the endothelium of the glomerular capillaries.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Staphylococcal vs Streptococcal TSS
statement: A 22-year-old female is admitted with high fever, hypotension, and a diffuse sunburn-like rash that later desquamates. Diagnostic criteria for Toxic Shock Syndrome are met. Laboratory evaluation reveals positive blood cultures for the causative organism. Which organism and clinical distinction are most likely?
options: Streptococcus pyogenes; blood cultures are typically positive in streptococcal TSS
Staphylococcus saprophyticus; the organism is typically bacitracin-sensitive
Streptococcus pyogenes; the syndrome is exclusively associated with tampon use
Staphylococcus aureus; the syndrome is typically associated with contaminated food
Staphylococcus aureus; blood cultures are typically positive in staphylococcal TSS
correctOption: Streptococcus pyogenes; blood cultures are typically positive in streptococcal TSS
optionExplanations: Streptococcal TSS (caused by S. pyogenes) usually presents with bacteremia, making blood cultures positive in many cases.
S. saprophyticus causes UTIs and is novobiocin-resistant; it is not a cause of TSS.
Streptococcal TSS is associated with skin/soft tissue infections; Staphylococcal TSS is the one classically linked to tampon use.
Staphylococcal TSS is associated with tampons or wound infections, while its enterotoxin causes food poisoning (a different syndrome).
In Staphylococcal TSS (mediated by TSST), blood cultures are typically negative because the disease is a toxemia, not a bacteremia.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 115 (Book Page): [S. pyogenes also causes another toxin-mediated disease, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome... However, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome typically has a recognizable site of pyogenic inflammation and blood cultures are often positive, whereas staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome typically has neither a site of pyogenic inflammation nor positive blood cultures.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A laboratory technician receives a clinical sample containing spherical gram-positive cocci. Which biochemical test should be performed first to differentiate whether the isolate belongs to the genus Staphylococcus or the genus Streptococcus?
options: Novobiocin resistance
Coagulase test
Mannitol fermentation
Bacitracin sensitivity
Catalase test
correctOption: Catalase test
optionExplanations: Novobiocin resistance is a secondary test used to distinguish between different species of coagulase-negative staphylococci, specifically identifying S. saprophyticus.
The coagulase test is used to differentiate Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci like S. epidermidis, but only after the genus is confirmed as Staphylococcus.
Mannitol fermentation is a screening characteristic primarily associated with Staphylococcus aureus to distinguish it from other staphylococcal species on Mannitol-Salt Agar.
Bacitracin sensitivity is specifically used to identify Group A streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes) after the isolate has been confirmed as a Streptococcus.
The catalase test is the primary biochemical differentiator between these genera; all staphylococci produce catalase (degrading H2O2), while all streptococci are catalase-negative.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 104 (Book Page): Biochemically, staphylococci produce catalase (i.e., they degrade hydrogen peroxide), whereas streptococci do not.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A 32-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with a high fever (103.5°F), pleuritic chest pain, and the production of blood-tinged 'rusty' sputum. A chest X-ray shows multiple cavitary lesions and areas of necrotizing pneumonia. Sputum Gram stain reveals Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Culture yields golden-yellow colonies that are coagulase-positive. Which virulence factor is most likely responsible for the severe necrotizing nature of this specific pulmonary infection?
options: P-V leukocidin
M protein
Protein A
Streptokinase
Teichoic acid
correctOption: P-V leukocidin
optionExplanations: Panton-Valentine (P-V) leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin that specifically targets white blood cells. Strains of S. aureus (especially CA-MRSA) that carry the lysogenic phage for this toxin cause aggressive necrotizing skin infections and a highly lethal necrotizing pneumonia characterized by cavitation.
M protein is the major antiphagocytic factor for S. pyogenes, not S. aureus.
Protein A inhibits phagocytosis by binding IgG but is not primarily known for causing the tissue necrosis and cavitation seen in severe pneumonia.
Streptokinase is a fibrinolysin produced by streptococci that dissolves clots; it is not a staphylococcal necrotizing toxin.
Teichoic acids facilitate adherence to mucosal cells but do not possess the cytotoxic activity required to cause necrotizing pneumonia.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): P-V leukocidin is an important virulence factor for CA-MRSA and plays a role in the severe SSTI caused by this organism. A severe necrotizing pneumonia is also caused by strains of S. aureus that produce P-V leukocidin.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Biochemical basis of the coagulase test.
statement: During a laboratory rotation, a student is asked to differentiate Staphylococcus aureus from Staphylococcus epidermidis using the coagulase test. Which of the following best describes the biochemical reaction observed in a positive test?
options: The organism produces a protein that enhances the zone of hemolysis produced by S. aureus.
Bacterial enzymes activate prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.
Bacterial catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide to produce visible oxygen bubbles.
The organism ferments mannitol, lowering the pH and changing the phenol red indicator to yellow.
The organism produces an enzyme that hydrolyzes hippurate, a characteristic of Group B Streptococci.
correctOption: Bacterial enzymes activate prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.
optionExplanations: This describes the CAMP test used to identify Group B Streptococci.
This accurately describes the mechanism of the coagulase enzyme, which mimics the host coagulation cascade to create a fibrin barrier around the bacteria.
This describes the catalase test, which is positive for all Staphylococci and negative for Streptococci.
This describes the mannitol fermentation test, which is a screening device for S. aureus, but is not the coagulase test.
This describes the hippurate hydrolysis test used for S. agalactiae.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 105 (Book Page)-119: S. aureus is distinguished from the others primarily by coagulase production (Figure 15–6). Coagulase is an enzyme that causes plasma to clot by activating prothrombin to form thrombin. Thrombin then catalyzes the activation of fibrinogen to form the fibrin clot.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Morphological examination of a Gram stain reveals spherical, Gram-positive cocci arranged in long chains. Biochemical testing shows the organism is catalase-negative. Which cell wall component is used to classify this organism into specific Lancefield groups?
options: M protein
Teichoic acid
C carbohydrate
Peptidoglycan
Lipoteichoic acid
correctOption: C carbohydrate
optionExplanations: M protein is used for 'typing' within Group A (S. pyogenes), but it does not determine the Lancefield group itself.
Teichoic acids are found in staphylococci (ribitol phosphate) and are part of the cell wall, but not used for Lancefield classification.
The C carbohydrate (an amino sugar in the cell wall) is the basis of the Lancefield classification (Groups A through U).
Peptidoglycan is the structural framework of the cell wall in all GPC, not a specific antigenic marker for grouping.
Lipoteichoic acid is found in both staph and strep and facilitates adherence (e.g., to pharyngeal epithelium), but is not the Lancefield group antigen.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 113 (Book Page): C carbohydrate determines the group of β-hemolytic streptococci. It is located in the cell wall, and its specificity is determined by an amino sugar.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcus aureus utilizes various cell wall components to evade the host immune system. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological mechanism by which Protein A functions as a virulence factor?
options: It facilitates adherence to mucosal cells via ribitol phosphate polymers
It acts as a protease to cleave desmoglein in cellular desmosomes
It binds the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the binding of phagocyte Fc receptors
It stimulates the release of IL-1 and TNF from macrophages to induce septic shock
It degrades the C3b component of complement to inhibit opsonization
correctOption: It binds the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the binding of phagocyte Fc receptors
optionExplanations: Adherence to mucosal cells is mediated by teichoic acids, which are ribitol phosphate polymers, rather than Protein A.
The cleavage of desmoglein in desmosomes is the mechanism of action for exfoliatin, the toxin responsible for scalded skin syndrome, not Protein A.

Protein A binds to the Fc region of IgG antibodies. Because the Fc region is sequestered by the bacterial cell wall protein, it is unavailable to bind to Fc receptors on the surface of neutrophils and macrophages, effectively blocking phagocytosis.
The stimulation of cytokines (IL-1, TNF) from macrophages is a property of lipoteichoic acids or superantigens like TSST-1, not Protein A.
Protein A does not directly degrade C3b; the inactivation of C3b is a mechanism associated with the M protein of S. pyogenes.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): Protein A is the major protein in the cell wall. It is an important virulence factor because it binds to the Fc portion of immunoglobulin (Ig) G. The Fc part is occupied and is not free to bind to the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages, so phagocytosis of S. aureus by those cells does not occur.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Mechanism of Protein A in immune evasion
statement: Staphylococcus aureus utilizes Protein A as a primary virulence factor to evade the host immune response. What is the specific mechanism by which this protein prevents phagocytosis?
options: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the Fc receptor on neutrophils from binding.
It cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, causing the epidermis to slough off.
It forms pores in the leukocyte cell membrane, causing loss of low-molecular-weight substances.
It activates prothrombin to form thrombin, creating a protective fibrin clot.
It acts as a superantigen to stimulate the release of massive amounts of IL-1 and IL-2.
correctOption: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the Fc receptor on neutrophils from binding.
optionExplanations: Protein A binds to the Fc region of IgG, which is the exact same site required by the Fc receptors on phagocytes (neutrophils/macrophages); by occupying this site, the bacterium prevents opsonization and subsequent phagocytosis.
Cleaving desmoglein in desmosomes is the mechanism of exfoliatin, which leads to Scalded Skin Syndrome, not the function of Protein A.
Forming pores in cell membranes is the mechanism of action of alpha toxin and P-V leukocidin, which directly kill white blood cells rather than interfering with opsonization molecules like Protein A.
Activating prothrombin to form thrombin is the mechanism of the enzyme coagulase, which helps wall off infections but is not the function of Protein A.
Acting as a superantigen to stimulate cytokines is characteristic of TSST and enterotoxin, which cause systemic shock or food poisoning.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): Protein A is the major protein in the cell wall. It is an important virulence factor because it binds to the Fc portion of immunoglobulin (Ig) G. category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A 10-year-old child presents with migratory polyarthritis and a new heart murmur several weeks after an untreated episode of pharyngitis. Which immunologic process best explains the development of this nonsuppurative sequela?
options: Molecular mimicry leading to an immunologic cross-reaction between M proteins and host tissue.
Direct invasion of heart and joint tissue by viable bacteria from the bloodstream.
Systemic release of superantigens causing massive cytokine production and hypotension.
Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane.
Exotoxin-mediated damage to cardiac myocytes via ADP-ribosylation.
correctOption: Molecular mimicry leading to an immunologic cross-reaction between M proteins and host tissue.
optionExplanations: Rheumatic fever is caused by molecular mimicry. Antibodies produced against the M protein of S. pyogenes cross-react with similar antigenic determinants on human heart valves, joint synovium, and brain tissue, leading to an autoimmune inflammatory response.
Rheumatic fever is a 'nonsuppurative' disease, meaning that the lesions are sterile and there is no direct bacterial invasion of the heart or joints at the time of symptoms.
This describes the mechanism of Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome, which is an acute toxin-mediated condition, not a delayed immunologic sequel like rheumatic fever.

This describes the pathogenesis of Acute Glomerulonephritis, which is also a poststreptococcal disease but results from Type III hypersensitivity, not the cross-reactive Type II mechanism of Rheumatic Fever.
ADP-ribosylation is a mechanism used by diphtheria and pertussis toxins, but not by Streptococcus pyogenes to cause rheumatic fever.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 117 (Book Page): Rheumatic fever is due to an immunologic cross-reaction between antibodies formed against M proteins of S. pyogenes and proteins on the surface of joint, heart, and brain tissue. It is an autoimmune disease greatly exacerbated by recurrent streptococcal infections.

statement: Which type of streptococcal hemolysis is characterized by an incomplete lysis of red blood cells, producing a distinct green zone around colonies on blood agar due to the oxidation of hemoglobin?
options: Gamma-hemolysis
Beta-hemolysis
Epsilon-hemolysis
Delta-hemolysis
Alpha-hemolysis
correctOption: Alpha-hemolysis
optionExplanations: Gamma-hemolysis is a misnomer referring to the complete absence of hemolytic activity, where no change is seen in the agar around the colonies.
Beta-hemolysis involves the complete lysis of red blood cells, resulting in a clear, transparent zone around the bacterial colonies.
Epsilon-hemolysis is not a recognized category for the Lancefield or hemolytic classification of human pathogenic streptococci.
Delta-hemolysis is not a standard classification term used for the medically important streptococci mentioned in the clinical text.
Alpha-hemolysis is the incomplete lysis of erythrocytes. The resulting green color is caused by the conversion of hemoglobin to biliverdin by peroxides produced by the bacteria.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 111 (Book Page): α-Hemolytic streptococci form a green zone around their colonies as a result of incomplete lysis of red blood cells in the agar. The green color is formed when hydrogen peroxide produced by the bacteria oxidizes hemoglobin (red color) to biliverdin (green color).

statement: Staphylococcus aureus employs Protein A as a major cell wall virulence factor. By which mechanism does this protein specifically impede the host immune response?

It activates prothrombin to thrombin, creating a protective fibrin clot.
It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils.
It cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, causing epidermal separation.
It degrades DNA in necrotic tissue to facilitate bacterial spread.
correctOption: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils.
optionExplanations: Superantigen activity is characteristic of Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin (TSST) and enterotoxins, which cause systemic cytokine storms rather than localized inhibition of phagocytosis.
Activation of prothrombin is the function of coagulase, which helps wall off infections but is not the role of Protein A.
Protein A binds to the Fc region of IgG antibodies. This prevents the antibody from orienting correctly for the Fc receptors on phagocytes, effectively blocking opsonization and phagocytosis.
Cleavage of desmoglein is the mechanism of action for exfoliatin, the toxin responsible for scalded skin syndrome, not Protein A.
Degrading DNA is the function of DNase (streptodornase), which is produced by group A streptococci to reduce the viscosity of pus.

statement: A specific protein found in the cell wall of Staphylococcus aureus functions as an essential virulence factor by interfering with the host's humoral immune response. Through what mechanism does this protein primarily inhibit the elimination of the bacteria?
options: It activates prothrombin to form thrombin, creating a fibrin clot that walls off the site from neutrophils.
It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the Fc receptor on phagocytes from initiating opsonization.
It cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, causing separation of the granular cell layer in the epidermis.
It degrades DNA in necrotic tissue to facilitate the spread of the organism through the skin.
It acts as a superantigen, stimulating massive release of IL-1 and IL-2 to induce toxic shock.
correctOption: It binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing the Fc receptor on phagocytes from initiating opsonization.
optionExplanations: This describes the function of coagulase, an enzyme that clots plasma.
Protein A binds to the Fc portion of IgG. This prevents the antibody from binding to the Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, effectively blocking phagocytosis.
This describes the mechanism of exfoliatin (scalded skin syndrome toxin), not Protein A.
This describes the function of DNase (streptodornase), which is typically associated with Group A Streptococci.
This describes the mechanism of Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin (TSST), which acts as a superantigen.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A 12-year-old male presents with high fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex. He had a severe sore throat three weeks prior that was untreated. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology of his current condition?
options: Proteolytic destruction of joint cartilage by Streptolysin O and S.
Immunologic cross-reaction between anti-M protein antibodies and cardiac myosin.
Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane.
Direct bacterial invasion of the endocardial tissue leading to vegetation formation.
A systemic toxemia caused by erythrogenic toxin acting as a superantigen.
correctOption: Immunologic cross-reaction between anti-M protein antibodies and cardiac myosin.
optionExplanations: Streptolysins are pore-forming toxins that kill phagocytes during the acute infection; they do not cause the delayed polyarthritis seen in rheumatic fever.
The M protein of S. pyogenes shares epitopes with cardiac myosin. Antibodies produced against the bacteria mistakenly attack heart and joint tissues.
This describes acute glomerulonephritis (Type III hypersensitivity), which usually follows skin infections or pharyngitis, not the cardiac manifestations of rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic fever is nonsuppurative; the heart damage is immunologic, and organisms are not present in the cardiac lesions.
Erythrogenic toxin causes the rash of scarlet fever, not the chronic valvular damage or joint pain of rheumatic fever.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 117 (Book Page): Rheumatic fever is due to an immunologic cross-reaction between antibodies formed against M proteins of S. pyogenes and proteins on the surface of joint, heart, and brain tissue.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
coreConcept: Primary Biochemical Differentiation of Gram-Positive Cocci
statement: A laboratory technician receives a swab from a skin abscess and performs a biochemical test to differentiate between the two most common genera of gram-positive cocci. Which enzyme production is consistently positive in all staphylococci but absent in all streptococci?
options: Fibrinolysin
Coagulase
Beta-lactamase
Hyaluronidase
Catalase
correctOption: Catalase
optionExplanations: Fibrinolysin (staphylokinase) is an enzyme produced by S. aureus that dissolves fibrin clots, but it is not a primary diagnostic marker for the entire genus and is shared by some streptococci (streptokinase).

Coagulase is produced by Staphylococcus aureus to clot plasma, but it is not produced by coagulase-negative staphylococci like S. epidermidis, thus it does not differentiate the entire genus from streptococci.
Beta-lactamase is an enzyme that degrades penicillins; while common in staphylococci (over 90%), it is also found in various other bacteria and is not a genus-defining biochemical characteristic.

Hyaluronidase, known as spreading factor, is produced by both Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes to degrade the ground substance of connective tissue, making it useless for genus differentiation.

Catalase is the definitive biochemical marker that distinguishes the genus Staphylococcus (positive) from the genus Streptococcus (negative). It functions by degrading hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, protecting the bacteria from oxidative burst within neutrophils.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 104 (Book Page): Biochemically, staphylococci produce catalase (i.e., they degrade hydrogen peroxide), whereas streptococci do not.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: The resistance of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) to beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins such as nafcillin is molecularly mediated by which specific change?
options: Inactivation of the drug by a plasmid-encoded enzyme
Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins in the cell membrane
Export of the drug via a plasmid-encoded transport pump
Substitution of d-lactate for d-alanine in the cell wall
Reduced uptake of the drug due to mutant porin proteins
correctOption: Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins in the cell membrane
optionExplanations: Standard penicillin resistance in S. aureus is mediated by beta-lactamase (enzymatic inactivation), but MRSA resistance overcomes even beta-lactamase-resistant drugs via PBP changes.
MRSA resistance is chromosomal (mecA gene) and involves the synthesis of PBP2a, an altered transpeptidase that does not bind beta-lactams, allowing the bacteria to continue cell wall synthesis.
Efflux pumps are mechanisms for tetracycline or fluoroquinolone resistance, but not the primary mechanism for methicillin resistance in S. aureus.
This is the mechanism of vancomycin resistance (substitution in peptidoglycan precursors), seen in VISA/VRSA and Enterococci.
Porin mutations are common mechanisms of resistance in Gram-negative bacteria like Pseudomonas, but not the mechanism for MRSA.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): Note, however, that many strains of S. aureus are resistant to the β-lactamase–resistant penicillins, such as methicillin and nafcillin, by virtue of changes in the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) in their cell membrane. Genes on the bacterial chromosome called mecA genes encode these altered PBPs.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A 12-year-old patient presents with symptoms of pharyngitis. A throat swab is cultured, yielding beta-hemolytic colonies. The organism is found to be sensitive to bacitracin. Which component of this organism is considered its most important virulence factor due to its antiphagocytic property and ability to inactivate C3b?
options: C carbohydrate
M protein
Hyaluronic acid capsule
Streptokinase
Lipoteichoic acid
correctOption: M protein
optionExplanations: The C carbohydrate is used for Lancefield grouping (identifying the organism as Group A) but is not the primary antiphagocytic virulence factor.
M protein is the major virulence factor of S. pyogenes. It is highly antiphagocytic and interferes with the complement cascade by inactivating C3b.
While S. pyogenes does have a hyaluronic acid capsule that retards phagocytosis, the text explicitly identifies M protein as the 'most important virulence factor'.
Streptokinase is an enzyme that activates plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve fibrin clots, facilitating the spread of the organism, but it is not primarily antiphagocytic.
Lipoteichoic acid facilitates adherence to pharyngeal epithelium via pili but does not inactivate C3b.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 113 (Book Page): M protein is the most important virulence factor of S. pyogenes . It protrudes from the outer surface of the cell and blocks phagocytosis (i.e., it is antiphagocytic). It inactivates C3b, a component of complement that opsonizes the bacteria prior to phagocytosis.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A woman with a urinary tract infection is found to have gram-positive cocci in clusters in her urine culture. The organism is catalase-positive and coagulase-negative. Which test is used to definitively identify this organism as Staphylococcus saprophyticus?
options: Ability to hydrolyze hippurate.
Solubility in bile salts.
Growth in the presence of bacitracin.
Resistance to the antibiotic novobiocin.
Sensitivity to the antibiotic novobiocin.
correctOption: Resistance to the antibiotic novobiocin.
optionExplanations: Hippurate hydrolysis is a marker for S. agalactiae.
Bile solubility is a test for S. pneumoniae.
Bacitracin is used for identifying S. pyogenes, not staphylococci.
S. saprophyticus is uniquely resistant to novobiocin among the common human staphylococcal pathogens, facilitating its identification.
Novobiocin sensitivity identifies S. epidermidis, which is a much less common cause of community-acquired UTI in young women.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): TABLE 15 – 1 Staphylococci of Medical Importance... S. saprophyticus ... Coagulase - ... Resistant to novobiocin.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by the systemic dissemination of an exotoxin. What is the specific enzymatic target of this toxin in human skin?
options: C3b component of complement, inhibiting opsonization.
Prothrombin, leading to localized intravascular coagulation.
Elongation factor-2, resulting in arrest of protein synthesis.
Hyaluronic acid, the ground substance of subcutaneous tissue.
Desmoglein in desmosomes, causing epidermal separation.
correctOption: Desmoglein in desmosomes, causing epidermal separation.
optionExplanations: This is the target inactivated by M protein of S. pyogenes and Protein A of S. aureus.
This is the function of staphylococcal coagulase.
This is the target of Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas Exotoxin A.
This is the target of hyaluronidase ('spreading factor'), an enzyme produced by S. pyogenes and S. aureus.
Exfoliatin is a protease that specifically breaks down the adhesion molecule desmoglein, causing the skin to slough off.

It is “epidermolytic” and acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in desmosomes, leading to the separation of the epidermis at the granular cell layer.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Alpha-hemolysis on blood agar is characterized by a green zone surrounding the bacterial colonies. What biochemical reaction is responsible for this specific color change?

Activation of prothrombin to thrombin causing plasma to clot.
Oxidation of hemoglobin to biliverdin by hydrogen peroxide.
Fermentation of mannitol lowering the pH of the medium.
Complete lysis of red blood cells by streptolysin O.

optionExplanations: Lysozyme is a host defense enzyme that kills bacteria; it is not produced by streptococci to cause hemolysis.
This describes the action of the enzyme coagulase, which is used to identify Staphylococcus aureus, not a hemolytic reaction.
In alpha-hemolysis, the bacteria produce H2O2 which reacts with hemoglobin, converting it to green biliverdin, signifying incomplete RBC destruction.
Mannitol fermentation is used to identify S. aureus on Mannitol-Salt Agar and causes the agar to turn yellow, but it is not the mechanism for hemolysis.
Complete lysis of red blood cells describes Beta-hemolysis, which results in a clear zone, not a green one.

The green color is formed when hydrogen peroxide produced by the bacteria oxidizes hemoglobin (red color) to biliverdin (green color).

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A 72-year-old man with a history of COPD presents with sudden onset of high fever, productive cough with 'rusty' colored sputum, and pleuritic chest pain. What is the primary virulence factor of the organism responsible for this clinical presentation?

M protein that inhibits C3b activation
Exfoliatin that cleaves desmosomes
A thick polysaccharide capsule that interferes with phagocytosis
IgG degrading enzyme that cleaves heavy chains

optionExplanations: Enterotoxins are characteristic of S. aureus and are involved in food poisoning, not pneumonia.
M protein is the primary virulence factor of S. pyogenes, not S. pneumoniae.
Exfoliatin is produced by S. aureus.
The polysaccharide capsule of S. pneumoniae is its most critical virulence factor, preventing phagocytic clearance in the absence of specific antibodies.
IgG degrading enzyme is a factor produced by S. pyogenes.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce an enzyme that clots plasma. By what direct biochemical action does this enzyme function?
options: It hydrolyzes hippurate to differentiate the isolate from Group A streptococci.
It acts as a protease that degrades the C3b component of complement.
It cleaves IgG heavy chains to prevent complement activation.
It degrades the hydrogen peroxide produced during aerobic metabolism.
It activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
correctOption: It activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
optionExplanations: Hippurate hydrolysis is used to identify Group B Streptococci (S. agalactiae).
M protein (of S. pyogenes) inactivates C3b; this is not the action of coagulase.
This describes the action of IgG-degrading enzyme produced by Group A Streptococci.
This describes the function of catalase, produced by all staphylococci.
Coagulase activates prothrombin into thrombin, which then catalyzes the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into an insoluble fibrin clot.

Coagulase is an enzyme that causes plasma to clot by activating prothrombin to form thrombin. Thrombin then catalyzes the activation of fibrinogen to form the fibrin clot.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician due to several 'honey-colored' crusted lesions around her mouth. She was treated for similar lesions two weeks ago. Today, she also has periorbital edema and her mother notes that her urine appears 'smoky.' Which of the following is the most likely immunologic mechanism for her kidney condition?
options: Antibodies against the M protein cross-reacting with glomerular basement membrane proteins.
Direct invasion of the kidney by the Gram-positive cocci via hematogenous spread.
Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane.
Cytotoxic T cells directly attacking the renal tubular cells.
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation within the renal parenchyma.
correctOption: Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane.
optionExplanations: This describes molecular mimicry, which is the mechanism for Acute Rheumatic Fever, not Glomerulonephritis.
Post-streptococcal diseases are 'nonsuppurative,' meaning they occur weeks after the local infection and are not caused by the direct presence of organisms in the organ.

Acute Glomerulonephritis is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction where circulating immune complexes (streptococcal antigen and IgG) deposit on the glomerular basement membrane, leading to inflammation and damage.
T-cell mediated damage is not the mechanism of PSGN; it is an immune complex disease.
IgE is involved in Type I hypersensitivity (allergies), not the nephritic syndrome seen after streptococcal infections.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 116 (Book Page): The disease [Acute Glomerulonephritis] is initiated by antigen–antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane . Complement is activated and C5a attracts neutrophils that secrete enzymes that damage the endothelium of the glomerular capillaries.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A laboratory is attempting to distinguish Streptococcus pneumoniae from Viridans group streptococci. Which set of diagnostic results would confirm the isolate is S. pneumoniae?
options: Alpha-hemolytic, not bile-soluble, and resistant to optochin
Catalase-positive and growth in 6.5% NaCl
Non-hemolytic and positive for hippurate hydrolysis
Alpha-hemolytic, bile-soluble, and inhibited by optochin
Beta-hemolytic and sensitive to bacitracin
correctOption: Alpha-hemolytic, bile-soluble, and inhibited by optochin
optionExplanations: This describes the diagnostic profile of the Viridans group streptococci, which are also alpha-hemolytic but resistant to optochin and not bile-soluble.
All streptococci are catalase-negative. Growth in 6.5% NaCl is a characteristic of Enterococcus (Group D).
This describes S. agalactiae (Group B), which is typically beta-hemolytic and positive for hippurate.
S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic, its growth is inhibited by the chemical optochin (P disk), and its colonies are dissolved by bile salts (bile-soluble).
This describes S. pyogenes (Group A Strep), not S. pneumoniae.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 114 (Book Page): (1) the growth of pneumococci is inhibited by optochin, whereas the growth of viridans streptococci is not inhibited; and (2) colonies of pneumococci dissolve when exposed to bile (bile-soluble), whereas colonies of viridans streptococci do not dissolve.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: In the laboratory identification of alpha-hemolytic streptococci, which combination of tests would accurately differentiate Streptococcus pneumoniae from the viridans group?
options: Inhibition of growth by optochin and solubility of colonies in bile
Coagulase production and mannitol fermentation
Bacitracin sensitivity and hippurate hydrolysis
Presence of Protein A and catalase positivity
Growth in 6.5% NaCl and esculin hydrolysis in the presence of bile
correctOption: Inhibition of growth by optochin and solubility of colonies in bile
optionExplanations: S. pneumoniae is uniquely sensitive to the chemical optochin and its cell wall is lysed by bile salts, whereas viridans streptococci are resistant to both.
Coagulase and mannitol fermentation are used to identify S. aureus, not streptococci.
Bacitracin sensitivity identifies S. pyogenes (Group A), and hippurate hydrolysis identifies S. agalactiae (Group B).
Protein A and catalase are markers for staphylococci; all streptococci are catalase-negative.
Growth in 6.5% NaCl identifies Enterococci, and bile-esculin hydrolysis identifies Group D streptococci.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 114 (Book Page): Pneumococci and viridans streptococci are distinguished in the clinical laboratory by two main criteria: (1) the growth of pneumococci is inhibited by optochin, whereas the growth of viridans streptococci is not inhibited; and (2) colonies of pneumococci dissolve when exposed to bile (bile-soluble), whereas colonies of viridans streptococci do not dissolve.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Which of the following streptococcal hemolysins is oxygen-labile and is used in a serologic test to provide evidence of a recent Streptococcus pyogenes infection in the diagnosis of rheumatic fever?
options: P-V leukocidin
Streptolysin O
Streptolysin S
Alpha-hemolysin
Erythrogenic toxin
correctOption: Streptolysin O
optionExplanations: P-V leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin of S. aureus, not S. pyogenes.

Streptolysin O is an oxygen-labile hemolysin produced by S. pyogenes. Because it is highly immunogenic, the detection of Anti-Streptolysin O (ASO) antibodies is a critical diagnostic tool for confirming recent infections linked to post-streptococcal sequelae like rheumatic fever.
Streptolysin S is oxygen-stable and responsible for surface hemolysis, but humans are tolerant to it and do not develop antibodies useful for diagnosis.
Alpha-hemolysin is a term usually applied to a Staphylococcus aureus toxin or the partial hemolysis seen in S. pneumoniae, not the specific diagnostic marker for Group A strep.
Erythrogenic toxin is the cause of the rash in scarlet fever; while it is produced by Group A strep, it is not the basis of the standard ASO diagnostic test.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 115 (Book Page): Streptolysin O is inactivated by oxygen whereas streptolysin S is stable to oxygen. ... Antibody to streptolysin O develops after infection by S. pyogenes. Presence of this antibody is used as evidence of prior infection by S. pyogenes in the diagnosis of rheumatic fever.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A laboratory technician is attempting to differentiate alpha-hemolytic colonies recovered from a patient's sputum. Which combination of results would definitively identify the isolate as Streptococcus pneumoniae rather than a member of the Viridans group?
options: Lysis by bile and inhibition of growth by optochin
Negative for catalase and chain-like arrangement on Gram stain
Growth in 6.5% NaCl and hydrolysis of esculin in bile
Production of a green zone of incomplete lysis on blood agar
Sensitivity to bacitracin and positive for hippurate hydrolysis
correctOption: Lysis by bile and inhibition of growth by optochin
optionExplanations: S. pneumoniae is uniquely bile-soluble and optochin-sensitive, unlike the Viridans group streptococci.
These are general characteristics of the genus Streptococcus and do not distinguish between species within the genus.
These results identify Enterococcus faecalis (Group D), not S. pneumoniae.
Both S. pneumoniae and Viridans streptococci produce alpha-hemolysis (green zone), so this does not differentiate them.
These results identify Streptococcus pyogenes and Streptococcus agalactiae, respectively, which are beta-hemolytic.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcus aureus is the classic cause of abscess formation. Which enzyme produced by the bacterium is most directly involved in walling off the infected site to prevent neutrophil access?
options: Hyaluronidase
Lipase
Fibrinolysin
Catalase
Coagulase
correctOption: Coagulase
optionExplanations: Hyaluronidase is known as the 'spreading factor' because it degrades the ground substance of connective tissue, facilitating bacterial invasion rather than walling it off.
Lipases are enzymes that degrade fats on the skin surface, providing nutrients and aiding colonization of the sebaceous glands, but they do not participate in the formation of the fibrin wall.
Fibrinolysin (staphylokinase) does the opposite; it lyses fibrin clots and thrombi, potentially aiding the spread of the infection.
Catalase allows the bacteria to survive the oxidative burst inside neutrophils by degrading H2O2, but it does not create the physical fibrin barrier of an abscess.
Coagulase activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot. This clot sequesters the bacteria, forming the classic walled-off lesion known as an abscess.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 107 (Book Page): Coagulase is an important virulence factor in the formation of an abscess. It causes formation of a fibrin clot that walls off the bacteria and prevents access of neutrophils to the site of infection.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: What is the biochemical basis for the Lancefield classification system used to categorize beta-hemolytic streptococci into groups such as A, B, and D?
options: The type of hemolytic enzyme (O or S) produced
The ability to hydrolyze esculin in the presence of bile
Antigenic differences in the M protein
The presence of a hyaluronic acid capsule
Specificity determined by an amino sugar in the C carbohydrate
correctOption: Specificity determined by an amino sugar in the C carbohydrate
optionExplanations: The type of hemolysis (alpha, beta, or gamma) is a preliminary classification, but the Lancefield group depends on cell wall antigens, not the specific hemolysin enzyme.
Bile-esculin hydrolysis is a diagnostic test for Group D organisms (enterococci and S. bovis), but it is a biochemical reaction, not the antigenic basis for the Lancefield grouping.
M protein determines the specific 'type' within a group (e.g., within Group A), but the 'group' itself is determined by the C carbohydrate.
A hyaluronic acid capsule is a specific virulence factor of many Group A strains (S. pyogenes) used to evade phagocytes, but it is not the basis of the A-U grouping system.
The Lancefield system classifies streptococci based on the antigenicity of the cell wall C carbohydrate, which is chemically defined by specific amino sugars.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 113 (Book Page): C carbohydrate determines the group of β-hemolytic streptococci. It is located in the cell wall, and its specificity is determined by an amino sugar. For example, group A β-hemolytic streptococci (S. pyogenes) are distinguished from group B β-hemolytic streptococci (S. agalactiae) because they have a different C carbohydrate.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: The Lancefield classification system, used to categorize beta-hemolytic streptococci into groups A through U, is based on antigenic differences in which bacterial component?
options: Teichoic acid
M protein
Lipopolysaccharide
Peptidoglycan
C carbohydrate
correctOption: C carbohydrate
optionExplanations: Teichoic acids are found in staphylococci and some streptococci but are the basis for adherence rather than Lancefield grouping.
M protein determines the 'type' of Group A streptococci (serotyping) and is the main virulence factor, but not the group antigen.
Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is the endotoxin found in Gram-negative bacteria; it is not present in the Gram-positive streptococci.
Peptidoglycan is a structural component of the cell wall common to almost all bacteria and is not used for specific classification of streptococci.
The C carbohydrate (or C substance) is a group-specific polysaccharide in the cell wall that allows the classification into Lancefield groups.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 113 (Book Page): C carbohydrate determines the group of beta-hemolytic streptococci. It is located in the cell wall, and its specificity is determined by an amino sugar. ... These are arranged into groups A–U (known as Lancefield groups) on the basis of antigenic differences in C carbohydrate.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A laboratory technologist receives a clinical specimen containing Gram-positive cocci. To distinguish whether the isolate belongs to the genus Staphylococcus or Streptococcus, which biochemical characteristic is most definitive?
options: The presence of a thick peptidoglycan layer containing teichoic acids.
The ability of the organism to form long chains in liquid media.
The capacity of the organism to resist decolorization by alcohol-acetone.
The production of catalase to degrade hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
The lack of flagellar proteins resulting in a nonmotile phenotype.
correctOption: The production of catalase to degrade hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
optionExplanations: Both genera are Gram-positive and possess thick peptidoglycan and teichoic acids; this does not differentiate them.
While staphylococci form clusters and streptococci form chains, microscopic arrangement is a morphological observation, not a biochemical reaction.
The ability to resist decolorization is the definition of being Gram-positive, which applies to both genera.
Catalase production is the hallmark biochemical test that distinguishes staphylococci (positive) from streptococci (negative).
Both genera are nonmotile and do not form spores, so motility cannot be used for differentiation.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 104 (Book Page): Biochemically, staphylococci produce catalase (i.e., they degrade hydrogen peroxide), whereas streptococci do not.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: An 8-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a 2-day history of migratory polyarthritis and a new-onset heart murmur. History reveals a severe untreated sore throat three weeks prior. Laboratory tests show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and a high ASO titer. What is the precise immunopathological mechanism for this patient's condition?
options: Immunologic cross-reaction between antibodies to M protein and cardiac tissue.
Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane.
Direct invasion of the myocardial tissue by Beta-hemolytic bacteria.
A superantigen-mediated release of IL-1 and TNF leading to systemic toxemia.
Release of erythrogenic toxin causing capillary damage and a diffuse macular rash.
correctOption: Immunologic cross-reaction between antibodies to M protein and cardiac tissue.
optionExplanations: The M protein of S. pyogenes induces antibodies that accidentally target similar host proteins on heart and joint tissues, leading to inflammation.
This describes the mechanism for Acute Glomerulonephritis, another post-streptococcal disease that is specifically mediated by immune complexes.
Rheumatic fever is a non-suppurative sequela; there are no organisms present in the heart or joint lesions.
This describes the mechanism of Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin (TSST) or Pyrogenic Exotoxin A, not the autoimmune mechanism of Rheumatic Fever.
This describes the pathogenesis of Scarlet Fever, characterized by a 'strawberry tongue' and skin rash, not the joint/heart involvement of Rheumatic Fever.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 117 (Book Page): Rheumatic fever is due to an immunologic cross-reaction between antibodies formed against M proteins of S. pyogenes and proteins on the surface of joint, heart, and brain tissue.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A neonate presents with signs of sepsis and meningitis at 48 hours of life. CSF Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. The clinician suspects Group B Streptococcus. Which laboratory test would most rapidly and specifically support the identification of Streptococcus agalactiae?
options: Bile solubility test
Growth in hypertonic (6.5%) saline
Hippurate hydrolysis test
Sensitivity to bacitracin disk
Inhibition by optochin disk
correctOption: Hippurate hydrolysis test
optionExplanations: Bile solubility is a test for S. pneumoniae; Group B streptococci are not bile-soluble.
Growth in 6.5% NaCl is characteristic of Enterococci (Group D), not Group B strep.
Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B) is differentiated from other streptococci by its ability to hydrolyze sodium hippurate and its positive CAMP test result.
Bacitracin sensitivity identifies S. pyogenes (Group A). S. agalactiae is typically bacitracin-resistant.
Optochin sensitivity is the hallmark of S. pneumoniae, not Group B strep.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 113 (Book Page): Group B streptococci (S. agalactiae) colonize the genital tract of some women and can cause neonatal meningitis and sepsis. They are usually bacitracin-resistant. They hydrolyze (break down) hippurate, an important diagnostic criterion.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Acute glomerulonephritis typically appears 2 to 3 weeks after a skin infection with specific nephritogenic strains of S. pyogenes. What is the precise immunopathologic initiator of the resulting glomerular damage?
options: Cross-reaction of anti-M protein antibodies with cardiac myosin
Antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane
Direct cytotoxic effect of Streptolysin O on the tubular epithelium
Exotoxin B-mediated proteolytic destruction of the basement membrane
Granulomatous inflammation induced by persistent intracellular bacteria
correctOption: Antigen-antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane
optionExplanations: This describes the mechanism of Acute Rheumatic Fever (molecular mimicry/Type II hypersensitivity), not Acute Glomerulonephritis.
AGN is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction. Immune complexes lodge in the glomeruli, activating complement and recruiting neutrophils that release tissue-damaging enzymes.
Streptolysin O is a pore-forming toxin involved in hemolysis and neutrophil death, but it is not the primary mediator of glomerular damage in AGN.
Exotoxin B is a protease linked to necrotizing fasciitis ('flesh-eating' disease), not the immune-complex mediated damage of AGN.
S. pyogenes is a pyogenic extracellular pathogen; it does not cause disease via chronic granulomatous inflammation or persistent intracellular residency.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 116 (Book Page): The disease is initiated by antigen–antibody complexes on the glomerular basement membrane. Complement is activated and C5a attracts neutrophils that secrete enzymes that damage the endothelium of the glomerular capillaries.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: The significant clinical challenge posed by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is primarily due to which pharmacological modification in the bacterium?
options: Production of a specialized beta-lactamase that specifically degrades methicillin
Plasmid-mediated substitution of D-lactate for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan
The failure to activate autolytic enzymes, leading to antibiotic tolerance
A mutation in the DNA gyrase gene preventing the binding of fluoroquinolones
Chromosomal mecA genes encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)
correctOption: Chromosomal mecA genes encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)
optionExplanations: Traditional beta-lactamase (penicillinase) degrades penicillin G but not beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like methicillin or nafcillin.
The substitution of D-lactate for D-alanine is the mechanism for vancomycin resistance (VRSA/VRE), not methicillin resistance.
Tolerance refers to organisms that are inhibited but not killed by an antibiotic; it is not the primary mechanism of resistance in MRSA.
Mutations in DNA gyrase mediate resistance to quinolones, which is a different class of drugs than the beta-lactams affected in MRSA.
MRSA resistance is not enzymatic; it results from a structural change in the target (PBP2a) which has a low affinity for almost all beta-lactam drugs.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 106 (Book Page): Genes on the bacterial chromosome called mecA genes encode these altered PBPs. The most important of these PBPs is PBP2a that can perform its transpeptidase function but does not bind penicillins.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: A patient presents with a fever and heart murmur suspicious for infective endocarditis. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic cocci in chains. Which diagnostic test result would suggest the presence of Viridans group streptococci rather than Streptococcus pneumoniae?
options: The organism shows a positive quellung reaction.
The organism is resistant to lysis by bile.
The colonies dissolve when exposed to bile.
The organism is catalase-positive.
The organism is inhibited by an optochin disk.
correctOption: The organism is resistant to lysis by bile.
optionExplanations: The quellung reaction identifies the capsular serotype of S. pneumoniae.
Viridans group streptococci are characterized by being optochin-resistant and bile-insoluble, differentiating them from S. pneumoniae.
Bile solubility is diagnostic for S. pneumoniae.
All Streptococci are catalase-negative.
Optochin sensitivity is diagnostic for S. pneumoniae.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 114 (Book Page): Pneumococci and viridans streptococci are distinguished in the clinical laboratory by two main criteria: (1) the growth of pneumococci is inhibited by optochin, whereas the growth of viridans streptococci is not inhibited; and (2) colonies of pneumococci dissolve when exposed to bile (bile-soluble), whereas colonies of viridans streptococci do not dissolve.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological and diagnostic (covering every aspect) aspects of Staphylococci, Streptococci, ,
statement: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS), primarily affecting young children, involves which specific pathological event?
options: Formation of holes in the cell membrane leading to loss of low-molecular-weight substances
Cleavage of the protein desmoglein in desmosomes by a protease exotoxin
Activation of prothrombin to form thrombin, resulting in localized fibrin clots
Creation of pores in white blood cell membranes by P-V leukocidin
Induction of cytokines via the binding of a superantigen to class II MHC proteins
correctOption: Cleavage of the protein desmoglein in desmosomes by a protease exotoxin
optionExplanations: This describes the action of Alpha toxin, which leads to tissue necrosis and hemolysis, but not the specific epidermolytic effect of SSSS.
Exfoliatin targets the granular layer of the epidermis by proteolytically cleaving desmoglein, which maintains cell-to-cell adhesion in desmosomes.
This describes the action of the enzyme coagulase, which helps wall off infections (abscesses), rather than causing skin sloughing.
